nodes.name: Linear independence of the non-trivial zeta zeroes over the rationals
nodes.statement: It is not known whether any non-trivial zeroes of the zeta-function are linearly dependent over the rationals. That is, no one has found an $N\geq 1$ and integers $c_{1}, \ldots, c_{N}$, not all zero, for which \begin{equation} \sum_{n=1}^{N} c_{n} \gamma_{n} = 0, \end{equation} where $\rho_{n} = \beta_{n} + i\gamma_{n}$ is the $n$th non-trivial zero of $\zeta(s)$.
nodes.statement_short: It is unknown whether any nonzero integer relation $\sum c_n\gamma_n=0$ holds among the non-trivial zeta zeroes.

nodes.name: Linear dependence relation among the zeta zeroes
nodes.statement: \begin{equation} \sum_{n=1}^{N} c_{n} \gamma_{n} = 0, \end{equation}

nodes.name: Mertens' conjecture
nodes.statement: Mertens' conjecture that $M(x) = \sum_{n\leq x} \mu(n) \leq x^{\frac{1}{2}}$, where $\mu(n)$ is the M\"{o}bius function.
nodes.statement_short: The Mertens function satisfies $M(x)\le\sqrt{x}$ for all $x$.

nodes.name: Ingham's implication: Mertens' conjecture forces linear dependencies
nodes.statement: Ingham showed that Mertens' conjecture implies that there are infinitely many linear dependencies as given in (\ref{lindep}).
conclusions: there are infinitely many linear dependencies as given in (\ref{lindep})

nodes.name: Disproof of Mertens' conjecture
nodes.statement: Mertens' conjecture was shown to be false by Odlyzko and te Riele in \cite{MertDis}.
conclusions: Mertens' conjecture was shown to be false

nodes.name: Bateman et al. `singly infinite' result
nodes.statement: Bateman et al.\ \cite{Bateman} proved a `singly infinite' result: Mertens' conjecture implies that there are infinitely many sums of the type (\ref{lindep}) in which the $c_{n}$ are integers, not all zero, $|c_{n}|\leq 2$, and at most one $c_{n} = \pm 2.$
nodes.statement_short: Mertens' conjecture forces infinitely many relations with coefficients bounded by $2$ and at most one $\pm2$.
conclusions: there are infinitely many sums of the type (\ref{lindep}) in which the $c_{n}$ are integers, not all zero, $|c_{n}|\leq 2$, and at most one $c_{n} = \pm 2.$

nodes.name: No linear dependencies among the first 20 zeroes
nodes.statement: Furthermore, they considered all of these permissible sums for $1\leq N \leq 20$ and showed that no linear dependencies exist.
assumptions: all of these permissible sums for $1\leq N \leq 20$

nodes.name: Contrapositive of the Bateman et al. result
nodes.statement: if there is no relation of the type (\ref{lindep}) for $|c_{n}| \leq 2$, then Mertens' conjecture is false.
assumptions: there is no relation of the type (\ref{lindep}) for $|c_{n}| \leq 2$

nodes.name: Bounds for $\limsup$ and $\liminf$ of $M(x)x^{-1/2}$
nodes.statement: \begin{equation*} \limsup_{x\rightarrow\infty} M(x) x^{-1/2} \geq 1.6383, \quad \liminf_{x\rightarrow\infty} M(x) x^{-1/2} \leq -1.6383. \end{equation*}
nodes.statement_short: $\limsup M(x)x^{-1/2}\ge 1.6383$ and $\liminf M(x)x^{-1/2}\le-1.6383$ — the paper's main quantitative disproof of Mertens' conjecture.

nodes.name: Kotnik and te Riele bounds
nodes.statement: $\limsup_{x\rightarrow\infty} M(x) x^{-1/2} \geq 1.218$ and $\liminf_{x\rightarrow\infty} M(x) x^{-1/2} \leq -1.229$

nodes.name: Equality of the new upper and lower bounds
nodes.statement: An added feature to the approach in this paper is that the bounds given in Theorem \ref{Ours} for the $\limsup$ and the $\liminf$ are equal.

nodes.name: Hypotheses on $g$, its Mellin transform $G$ and the principal part $H$
nodes.statement: Suppose $g(x)$ is a piecewise-continuous real function that is bounded on finite intervals. Suppose also that \begin{equation} G(s) = \int_{1}^{\infty} g(x) x^{-s-1}\, dx \end{equation} originally absolutely convergent for $\sigma > \sigma_{a}$, say, can be continued analytically to $\sigma = \sigma_{0}$. Moreover, assume that one can write the principal part of $G(s)$ as \begin{equation} H(s) = G(s) - \left( \frac{r_{0}}{s- \sigma_{0}} + \sum_{\gamma} \frac{r_{\gamma}}{s- (\sigma_{0} + i\gamma)}\right), \end{equation} where $H(s)$ is analytic for $s= \sigma_{0} + it$, where $|t|<T$. Here, $\gamma$ is an element of some finite set of numbers $0 < |\gamma| <T$.
nodes.statement_short: $g$ is piecewise continuous and locally bounded, its transform $G$ continues to $\sigma_0$, and subtracting the poles at $\sigma_0$ and $\sigma_0+i\gamma$ leaves $H$ analytic on $|t|<T$.

nodes.name: Mellin-type transform $G(s)$ of $g$
nodes.statement: \begin{equation} G(s) = \int_{1}^{\infty} g(x) x^{-s-1}\, dx \end{equation}

nodes.name: Principal-part decomposition $H(s)$
nodes.statement: \begin{equation} H(s) = G(s) - \left( \frac{r_{0}}{s- \sigma_{0}} + \sum_{\gamma} \frac{r_{\gamma}}{s- (\sigma_{0} + i\gamma)}\right), \end{equation}

nodes.name: Ingham's Theorem 1
nodes.statement: for any $T>0$ and any $x_{0}$, \begin{equation} \liminf_{x\rightarrow\infty} \frac{g(x)}{x^{\sigma_{0}}} \leq r_{0} + \sum_{-T < \gamma < T} r_{\gamma} \left(1- \frac{|\gamma|}{T}\right) x_{0}^{i\gamma} \leq \limsup_{x\rightarrow\infty} \frac{g(x)}{x^{\sigma_{0}}}. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: A Fejér-kernel-weighted sum of the residues $r_\gamma$ is squeezed between $\liminf g(x)/x^{\sigma_0}$ and $\limsup g(x)/x^{\sigma_0}$.

nodes.name: Aligning the arguments of $x_0^{i\gamma}$ via Kronecker's theorem
nodes.statement: To exhibit large negative values of $\liminf_{x\rightarrow\infty} \frac{g(x)}{x^{\sigma_{0}}}$, for example, one hopes to align the arguments of the complex terms $x_{0}^{i\gamma}$ so that they all pull in the same direction. If the numbers $\gamma$ are independent one can achieve this using Kronecker's theorem.

nodes.name: Grosswald's weakening of linear independence
nodes.statement: Grosswald's idea is to extract some partial information by weakening the hypothesis that the $\gamma$s are linearly independent. This weaker version of linear independence has also been considered by Anderson and Stark \cite{AndStark} and Diamond \cite{Diamond}. The following version is that given in \cite{AndStark}.

nodes.name: The sets $\Gamma$, $\Gamma'$ and the integers $\{N_{\gamma}\}$
nodes.statement: Let $T>0$, and let $\Gamma$ denote a set of positive numbers. Define $\Gamma'$ as a subset of $\Gamma$ such that every $\gamma\in\Gamma'$ lies in the range $0< \gamma< T$. Finally, let $\{N_{\gamma}\}$ be a set of positive integers defined for $\gamma \in \Gamma'$.

nodes.name: $\{N_{\gamma}\}$-independence in $\Gamma \cap [0, T]$
nodes.statement: The elements of $\Gamma'$ are $\{N_{\gamma}\}$-independent in $\Gamma \cap [0, T]$ if \begin{equation} \sum_{\gamma\in\Gamma'} c_{\gamma} \gamma = 0, \quad \textrm{with } |c_{\gamma}| \leq N_{\gamma}, \end{equation} implies that all $c_{\gamma} = 0$ and for any $\gamma^{*}\in \Gamma \cap [0, T]$, \begin{equation} \sum_{\gamma\in\Gamma'} c_{\gamma} \gamma = \gamma^{*}, \quad \textrm{with } |c_{\gamma}| \leq N_{\gamma}, \end{equation} implies that $\gamma^{*} \in \Gamma'$, that $c_{\gamma*} = 1$, and that all other $c_{\gamma} = 0$.
nodes.statement_short: No bounded-coefficient relation among $\Gamma'$ vanishes nontrivially, and any bounded-coefficient representation of a $\gamma^*\in\Gamma\cap[0,T]$ is the trivial one.
differentia: \sum_{\gamma\in\Gamma'} c_{\gamma} \gamma = \gamma^{*}, \quad \textrm{with } |c_{\gamma}| \leq N_{\gamma}, \end{equation} implies that $\gamma^{*} \in \Gamma'$, that $c_{\gamma*} = 1$, and that all other $c_{\gamma} = 0$.

nodes.name: Vanishing bounded-coefficient relation
nodes.statement: \begin{equation} \sum_{\gamma\in\Gamma'} c_{\gamma} \gamma = 0, \quad \textrm{with } |c_{\gamma}| \leq N_{\gamma}, \end{equation}

nodes.name: Bounded-coefficient representation of $\gamma^{*}$
nodes.statement: \begin{equation} \sum_{\gamma\in\Gamma'} c_{\gamma} \gamma = \gamma^{*}, \quad \textrm{with } |c_{\gamma}| \leq N_{\gamma}, \end{equation}

nodes.name: Anderson and Stark theorem
nodes.statement: If the elements of $\Gamma'$ are $\{N_{\gamma}\}$-independent in $\Gamma \cap[0,T]$, then \begin{equation} \liminf_{x\rightarrow\infty} \frac{g(x)}{x^{\sigma_{0}}} \leq r_{0} - \sum_{\gamma \in \Gamma'} \frac{2N_{\gamma}}{N_{\gamma} + 1} |r_{\gamma}| \left(1- \frac{\gamma}{T}\right) \end{equation} and \begin{equation} \limsup_{x\rightarrow\infty} \frac{g(x)}{x^{\sigma_{0}}} \geq r_{0} + \sum_{\gamma \in \Gamma'} \frac{2N_{\gamma}}{N_{\gamma} + 1} |r_{\gamma}| \left(1- \frac{\gamma}{T}\right). \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Under $\{N_\gamma\}$-independence, $\liminf$ and $\limsup$ of $g(x)/x^{\sigma_0}$ are bounded by $r_0\mp\sum_{\gamma\in\Gamma'}\frac{2N_\gamma}{N_\gamma+1}|r_\gamma|(1-\gamma/T)$.

nodes.name: Ingham's classical result on $M(x)/\sqrt{x}$
nodes.statement: Ingham \cite[pp.\ 318-319]{Ingham1942} gave a proof of the classical result that \begin{equation} \liminf_{x\rightarrow \infty} \frac{M(x)}{\sqrt{x}} = -\infty, \quad\quad \limsup_{x\rightarrow \infty} \frac{M(x)}{\sqrt{x}} = \infty. \end{equation} follows if either the Riemann hypothesis is false or not all the zeroes are simple.
nodes.statement_short: If RH is false or some zero is not simple, then $M(x)/\sqrt{x}$ has $\liminf=-\infty$ and $\limsup=+\infty$.
assumptions: either the Riemann hypothesis is false or not all the zeroes are simple

nodes.name: Riemann hypothesis and simplicity of the zeroes
nodes.statement: Henceforth we assume the Riemann hypothesis and the simplicity of the zeroes.

nodes.name: Specialization to $g(x)=M(x)$, $\sigma_0=1/2$
nodes.statement: In (\ref{bigg}), take $g(x) = M(x)$ and so $\sigma_{0} = \frac{1}{2}$ and, in (\ref{bigg2}), $r_{0} = 0$ and $r_{\gamma} = (\rho\zeta'(\rho))^{-1}.$ Here $\rho = \frac{1}{2} + i\gamma$ is a typical non-trivial zero of the zeta-function.
nodes.statement_short: Apply the framework with $g=M$, $\sigma_0=1/2$, $r_0=0$ and $r_\gamma=(\rho\zeta'(\rho))^{-1}$.

nodes.name: Ingham's Theorem A
nodes.statement: Ingham \cite[Thm.\ A]{Ingham1942} used (\ref{InghamThm1}) to show that if the zeroes $\gamma$ are linearly independent, then (\ref{LastIn}) is true.

nodes.name: Grosswald's choice of $\Gamma'$ and $T$
nodes.statement: Let $M \geq 1$ be given. Choose $\Gamma' = \{\gamma_{1}, \ldots, \gamma_{M}\}$ and choose $T = \gamma_{L+1}-\epsilon$ for some small $\epsilon$, where $L \geq M$. Thus, $\Gamma\cap [0,T] = \{\gamma_{1}, \ldots, \gamma_{L}\}$.
nodes.statement_short: Take $\Gamma'$ to be the first $M$ zeroes and $T=\gamma_{L+1}-\epsilon$, so $\Gamma\cap[0,T]$ is the first $L$ zeroes.

nodes.name: Grosswald-type lower bound for $\liminf M(x)x^{-1/2}$
nodes.statement: \begin{equation} \liminf_{x\rightarrow\infty} \frac{M(x)}{x^{1/2}} \leq - \sum_{n=1}^{M} \frac{2N_{\gamma_{n}}}{N_{\gamma_{n}} + 1} \frac{1}{|\rho_{n} \zeta'(\rho_{n})|} \left(1- \frac{\gamma_{n}}{T}\right) \end{equation}

nodes.name: Grosswald-type upper bound for $\limsup M(x)x^{-1/2}$
nodes.statement: \begin{equation} \limsup_{x\rightarrow\infty} \frac{M(x)}{x^{1/2}} \geq \sum_{n=1}^{M} \frac{2N_{\gamma_{n}}}{N_{\gamma_{n}} + 1} \frac{1}{|\rho_{n} \zeta'(\rho_{n})|} \left(1- \frac{\gamma_{n}}{T}\right). \end{equation}

nodes.name: LLL-reduction
nodes.statement: Previous disproofs of Mertens' conjecture have utilized the basis reduction algorithm first described by Lenstra, Lenstra and Lov\'asz in \cite{lll}, called LLL-reduction.
nodes.statement_short: Lattice basis reduction producing a nearly orthogonal basis of a given lattice.

nodes.name: All $N_{\gamma_{n}}$ are equal
nodes.statement: We will also assume that all $N_{\gamma_{n}}$s are equal, and we denote their value by $N_{\gamma}$.

nodes.name: Main algorithm returning an appropriate value for $N_\gamma$
nodes.statement: \textbf{Input:} $(k,n,T) \in \mathbb{Z} \times \mathbb{Z} \times \mathbb{R}$.\\ \textbf{Output:} $N_\gamma$. \begin{enumerate} \item Define $K := 10^k$ and $m := \left|\Gamma \cap [0,T]\right|$. \item Compute all zeroes, $\gamma$, such that $0 <\gamma \leq T$ to at least $k$ decimal digits of precision. \item Sort the elements of $\Gamma \cap [0,T]$ using $\prec$ in (\ref{heavy-order}). Label the {\it heaviest} element $\gamma_1$, the next {\it heaviest} element $\gamma_2$, $\ldots$ , and the least {\it heavy} element $\gamma_m$. \item Define $\Gamma' := \left\{\gamma_1,\gamma_2, \cdots , \gamma_n\right\}$. \item Let $L_0$ be the reduced lattice basis obtained by running $L(K;\Gamma')$ through LLL-reduction. \item Apply Lemma \ref{gram} along with the contrapositive of Lemma \ref{cond1} to $L_0$ to get a candidate for $N_\gamma$. \item For all $n < t \leq m$, let $L_t$ be the reduced lattice basis obtained from running $L\left(K;\Gamma' \cup \left\{\gamma_t\right\}\right)$ through LLL-reduction. \item Apply Lemma \ref{gram} with the contrapositive of Lemma \ref{cond2} to every $L_t$ to get $m-n$ additional candidates for $N_\gamma$. \item Set $N_\gamma$ to be the minimum of all of the candidates for $N_\gamma$ that were computed in steps 6 and 8. \end{enumerate} \caption{Returns an appropriate value for $N_\gamma$ that satisfies the conditions laid out in (\ref{ind1}) and (\ref{ind2}).}
nodes.statement_short: Compute and weight-sort the zeroes below $T$, LLL-reduce $L(K;\Gamma')$ and each $L(K;\Gamma'\cup\{\gamma_t\})$, and return the minimum candidate $N_\gamma$.

nodes.name: Define $K$ and $m$
nodes.statement: \item Define $K := 10^k$ and $m := \left|\Gamma \cap [0,T]\right|$.
nodes.statement_short: Set the truncation scale $K=10^k$ and count the zeroes below $T$.

nodes.name: Compute the zeroes to $k$ digits
nodes.statement: \item Compute all zeroes, $\gamma$, such that $0 <\gamma \leq T$ to at least $k$ decimal digits of precision.
nodes.statement_short: Compute every zero in $(0,T]$ to at least $k$ decimal digits.

nodes.name: Sort the zeroes by heaviness
nodes.statement: \item Sort the elements of $\Gamma \cap [0,T]$ using $\prec$ in (\ref{heavy-order}). Label the {\it heaviest} element $\gamma_1$, the next {\it heaviest} element $\gamma_2$, $\ldots$ , and the least {\it heavy} element $\gamma_m$.
nodes.statement_short: Order $\Gamma\cap[0,T]$ by the weight ordering $\prec$, heaviest first.

nodes.name: Select $\Gamma'$
nodes.statement: \item Define $\Gamma' := \left\{\gamma_1,\gamma_2, \cdots , \gamma_n\right\}$.
nodes.statement_short: Take $\Gamma'$ to be the $n$ heaviest zeroes.

nodes.name: LLL-reduce $L(K;\Gamma')$
nodes.statement: \item Let $L_0$ be the reduced lattice basis obtained by running $L(K;\Gamma')$ through LLL-reduction.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce the lattice $L(K;\Gamma')$ to obtain the basis $L_0$.

nodes.name: First candidate for $N_\gamma$
nodes.statement: \item Apply Lemma \ref{gram} along with the contrapositive of Lemma \ref{cond1} to $L_0$ to get a candidate for $N_\gamma$.
nodes.statement_short: Combine the Gram–Schmidt bound with the contrapositive of Lemma 1 on $L_0$.

nodes.name: LLL-reduce each augmented lattice $L_t$
nodes.statement: \item For all $n < t \leq m$, let $L_t$ be the reduced lattice basis obtained from running $L\left(K;\Gamma' \cup \left\{\gamma_t\right\}\right)$ through LLL-reduction.
nodes.statement_short: For each remaining zero $\gamma_t$, reduce $L(K;\Gamma'\cup\{\gamma_t\})$.

nodes.name: Additional candidates from each $L_t$
nodes.statement: \item Apply Lemma \ref{gram} with the contrapositive of Lemma \ref{cond2} to every $L_t$ to get $m-n$ additional candidates for $N_\gamma$.
nodes.statement_short: Combine the Gram–Schmidt bound with the contrapositive of Lemma 2 on every $L_t$.

nodes.name: Take the minimum candidate
nodes.statement: \item Set $N_\gamma$ to be the minimum of all of the candidates for $N_\gamma$ that were computed in steps 6 and 8.
nodes.statement_short: Return the smallest of all candidate values of $N_\gamma$.

nodes.name: Why steps 6 and 8 guarantee the two independence conditions
nodes.statement: Note that by taking the minimum of all candidate values of $N_\gamma$, step 6 ensures that (\ref{ind1}) will be satisified. Moreover, step 6 ensures that (\ref{ind2}) will be satisfied when we consider $\gamma^* \in \Gamma'$ and step 8 ensures that (\ref{ind2}) will be satisfied when we consider $\gamma^* \not\in \Gamma'$.

nodes.name: The lattice $L(K;S)$
nodes.statement: Let $K \in \mathbb{Z}, S=\left\{\gamma_1,\cdots,\gamma_n\right\} \subset \mathbb{R}$ and define $\gamma_i'$ such that $K\gamma_i'=\lfloor K\gamma_i\rfloor$. Then $L(K;S) \subset \mathbb{Z}^{n+1}$ is the lattice generated by the following vectors $$\left(\begin{array}{c}1\\ 0 \\ \vdots \\ 0 \\ K\gamma_1'\end{array}\right), \left(\begin{array}{c}0\\ 1 \\ \vdots \\ 0 \\ K\gamma_2'\end{array}\right), \cdots , \left(\begin{array}{c}0\\ \vdots \\ 0 \\ 1 \\ K\gamma_n'\end{array}\right).$$
nodes.statement_short: The lattice in $\mathbb{Z}^{n+1}$ spanned by the standard basis vectors each augmented with the truncated value $K\gamma_i'$.

nodes.name: General form of a vector in $L(K;S)$
nodes.statement: $$a_1\left(\begin{array}{c}1\\ 0 \\ \vdots \\ 0 \\ K\gamma_1'\end{array}\right) +a_2\left(\begin{array}{c}0\\ 1 \\ \vdots \\ 0 \\ K\gamma_2'\end{array}\right) +\cdots +a_n\left(\begin{array}{c}0\\ \vdots \\ 0 \\ 1 \\ K\gamma_n'\end{array}\right) = \left(\begin{array}{c}a_1\\ a_2 \\ \vdots \\ a_n \\ Kx\end{array}\right),$$ where $x = a_1\gamma_1'+a_2\gamma_2'+\cdots+a_n\gamma_n'$.
nodes.statement_short: Every lattice vector is $(a_1,\dots,a_n,Kx)$ with $x=\sum a_i\gamma_i'$.

nodes.name: $N_\gamma$-dependent and $N_\gamma$-independent sets
nodes.statement: A set $S = \left\{\gamma_1,\gamma_2, \cdots, \gamma_n\right\} \subset \mathbb{R}$ is said to be $N_\gamma$-dependent if there exists $\alpha_1,\alpha_2,\cdots,\alpha_n \in \mathbb{R}$, not all zero, such that $\alpha_1\gamma_1+\cdots+\alpha_n\gamma_n= 0$ with $|\alpha_i| \leq N_\gamma$. $S$ is said to be $N_\gamma$-independent if it is not $N_\gamma$-dependent.
nodes.statement_short: $S$ is $N_\gamma$-dependent if some nonzero real coefficients bounded by $N_\gamma$ annihilate it; independent otherwise.
differentia: there exists $\alpha_1,\alpha_2,\cdots,\alpha_n \in \mathbb{R}$, not all zero, such that $\alpha_1\gamma_1+\cdots+\alpha_n\gamma_n= 0$ with $|\alpha_i| \leq N_\gamma$

nodes.name: Weakly $N_\gamma$-dependent and weakly $N_\gamma$-independent sets
nodes.statement: A set $S = \left\{\gamma_1,\gamma_2, \cdots, \gamma_n\right\} \subset \mathbb{R}$ is said to be weakly $N_\gamma$-dependent if there exists $\alpha_1,\alpha_2,\cdots,\alpha_n \in \mathbb{R}$, not all zero, such that $\alpha_1\gamma_1+\cdots+\alpha_n\gamma_n= 0$ with $|\alpha_i| \leq N_\gamma+1$ with at most one $i$ such that $|\alpha_i| = N_\gamma+1$. $S$ is said to be weakly $N_\gamma$-independent if it is not weakly $N_\gamma$-dependent.
nodes.statement_short: Same as $N_\gamma$-dependence but coefficients may reach $N_\gamma+1$ in at most one coordinate.
differentia: there exists $\alpha_1,\alpha_2,\cdots,\alpha_n \in \mathbb{R}$, not all zero, such that $\alpha_1\gamma_1+\cdots+\alpha_n\gamma_n= 0$ with $|\alpha_i| \leq N_\gamma+1$ with at most one $i$ such that $|\alpha_i| = N_\gamma+1$

nodes.name: Warning about the two notions of independence
nodes.statement: We wish to alert the reader to the potential confusion between $\{N_\gamma\}$-independent (from Definition \ref{defcon1}) and $N_\gamma$-independent (from Definition \ref{lin-dep}).

nodes.name: Short lattice vector from weak $N_\gamma$-dependence
nodes.statement: If $S = \left\{\gamma_1,\gamma_2, \cdots, \gamma_n\right\} \subset \mathbb{R}$ is weakly $N_\gamma$-dependent, then there exists a nonzero vector $v\in L(K;S)$ such that $|v|^2 < (n^2+n)N_{\gamma}^2+(2n+2)N_{\gamma}+2$.
nodes.statement_short: Weak $N_\gamma$-dependence of $S$ forces a nonzero vector of $L(K;S)$ of squared length below $(n^2+n)N_\gamma^2+(2n+2)N_\gamma+2$.
conclusions: there exists a nonzero vector $v\in L(K;S)$ such that $|v|^2 < (n^2+n)N_{\gamma}^2+(2n+2)N_{\gamma}+2$

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 1
nodes.statement: Consider the following vector $v \in L(K;S),$ $$v=\left(\begin{array}{c}\alpha_1\\ \alpha_2 \\ \vdots \\ \alpha_n \\ K(\alpha_1\gamma_1'+\cdots+\alpha_n\gamma_n')\end{array}\right).$$ The assumptions of the lemma show \begin{equation*} \begin{split} |v|^2&=\alpha_i^2+\cdots+\alpha_n^2+K^2(\alpha_1\gamma_1'+\cdots+\alpha_n\gamma_n')^2 \\ &= \alpha_i^2+\cdots+\alpha_n^2+K^2\{(\alpha_1\gamma_1'+\cdots+\alpha_n\gamma_n')-(\alpha_1\gamma_1+\cdots+\alpha_n\gamma_n)\}^{2}, \end{split} \end{equation*} since $\alpha_1\gamma_1+\cdots+\alpha_n\gamma_n= 0$. Upon using the upper bounds on $|\alpha_{i}|$ and the fact that $|\gamma_{i} - \gamma_{i}'| < K^{-1}$, it follows that \begin{equation*} |v|^{2} < nN_{\gamma}^2+2N_{\gamma}+1+K^2\left(\frac{nN_{\gamma}+1}{K}\right)^2, \end{equation*} whence the lemma follows.
nodes.statement_short: Construct the lattice vector with coordinates $\alpha_i$, expand $|v|^2$ using $\sum\alpha_i\gamma_i=0$, then bound it with $|\alpha_i|$ and $|\gamma_i-\gamma_i'|<K^{-1}$.

nodes.name: Construct the candidate lattice vector
nodes.statement: Consider the following vector $v \in L(K;S),$ $$v=\left(\begin{array}{c}\alpha_1\\ \alpha_2 \\ \vdots \\ \alpha_n \\ K(\alpha_1\gamma_1'+\cdots+\alpha_n\gamma_n')\end{array}\right).$$
nodes.statement_short: Exhibit $v\in L(K;S)$ whose first $n$ coordinates are the dependence coefficients $\alpha_i$.

nodes.name: Expand $|v|^2$ using the vanishing relation
nodes.statement: The assumptions of the lemma show \begin{equation*} \begin{split} |v|^2&=\alpha_i^2+\cdots+\alpha_n^2+K^2(\alpha_1\gamma_1'+\cdots+\alpha_n\gamma_n')^2 \\ &= \alpha_i^2+\cdots+\alpha_n^2+K^2\{(\alpha_1\gamma_1'+\cdots+\alpha_n\gamma_n')-(\alpha_1\gamma_1+\cdots+\alpha_n\gamma_n)\}^{2}, \end{split} \end{equation*} since $\alpha_1\gamma_1+\cdots+\alpha_n\gamma_n= 0$.
nodes.statement_short: Rewrite $|v|^2$ as a truncation error by subtracting the vanishing sum $\sum\alpha_i\gamma_i=0$.

nodes.name: Bound the truncation error and conclude
nodes.statement: Upon using the upper bounds on $|\alpha_{i}|$ and the fact that $|\gamma_{i} - \gamma_{i}'| < K^{-1}$, it follows that \begin{equation*} |v|^{2} < nN_{\gamma}^2+2N_{\gamma}+1+K^2\left(\frac{nN_{\gamma}+1}{K}\right)^2, \end{equation*} whence the lemma follows.
nodes.statement_short: Insert $|\alpha_i|\le N_\gamma+1$ and $|\gamma_i-\gamma_i'|<K^{-1}$ to obtain the stated bound.

nodes.name: Short lattice vector from $N_\gamma$-dependence with an outside zero
nodes.statement: If $S = \left\{\gamma_1,\gamma_2, \cdots, \gamma_n,\gamma_t\right\} \subset \mathbb{R}$ is $N_\gamma$-dependent where $\gamma_t \not\in\Gamma'$ is a zero, then there exists a nonzero vector $v\in L(K;S)$ such that $|v|^2 < (n^2+n)N_{\gamma}^2+2nN_{\gamma}+2$.
nodes.statement_short: $N_\gamma$-dependence of $\Gamma'$ together with an outside zero $\gamma_t$ forces a short nonzero vector in $L(K;S)$.
conclusions: there exists a nonzero vector $v\in L(K;S)$ such that $|v|^2 < (n^2+n)N_{\gamma}^2+2nN_{\gamma}+2$

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 2
nodes.statement: The proof follows that of Lemma \ref{cond1}; for each $i$, we have $|\alpha_{i}| \leq N_\gamma$.
nodes.statement_short: Repeat the proof of Lemma 1 with the uniform bound $|\alpha_i|\le N_\gamma$.

nodes.name: The lemma bounds are independent of $K$
nodes.statement: Note that in both lemmas above, the bounds are independent of our choice of $K$. The following lemma is true of all lattices.

nodes.name: Gram--Schmidt lower bound for nonzero lattice vectors
nodes.statement: Let $L \subset \mathbb{Z}^n$ be a lattice of dimension $m$. Let $\{b_i^*\}$ be the Gram--Schmidt orthogonalization of the basis of $L$. Then $|x|^2 \geq \min\left(|b_i^*|^2\right)$ for any nonzero $x \in L$.
assumptions: $\{b_i^*\}$ be the Gram--Schmidt orthogonalization of the basis of $L$

nodes.name: Sufficient Gram--Schmidt condition for $\{N_\gamma\}$-independence
nodes.statement: Let $L_0 = L(K;\Gamma')$ and let $L_t = L(K;\Gamma' \cup \{\gamma_t\})$ where $\gamma_t \in (\Gamma \cap [0,T]) \setminus \Gamma'$. We define $\left\{b_1,\cdots,b_n\right\}$ and $\left\{\beta_{t,1},\cdots,\beta_{t,n},\beta_{t,t}\right\}$ to be a basis for each lattice, respectively. The elements of $\Gamma'$ are $\{N_{\gamma}\}$-independent in $\Gamma \cap [0, T]$ if $$\min\left(|b_i^*|^2\right) \geq (n^2+n)N_{\gamma}^2+(2n+2)N_{\gamma}+2$$ and $$\min\left(|\beta_{t,i}^*|^2\right) \geq (n^2+n)N_{\gamma}^2+2nN_{\gamma}+2$$ for all $\gamma_t \in (\Gamma \cap [0,T]) \setminus \Gamma'$.
nodes.statement_short: $\Gamma'$ is $\{N_\gamma\}$-independent whenever the Gram–Schmidt minima of $L_0$ and of every $L_t$ exceed the Lemma 1 and Lemma 2 bounds.
conclusions: The elements of $\Gamma'$ are $\{N_{\gamma}\}$-independent in $\Gamma \cap [0, T]$

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 3
nodes.statement: We have two conditions to check. The first, (\ref{ind1}), is taken as a direct consequence of Lemma \ref{gram} and the contrapositive of Lemma \ref{cond1}. (\ref{ind2}) must be broken up into two separate parts. If $\gamma^* \in \Gamma'$, then we may apply the contrapositive of Lemma \ref{cond1} again. However, if $\gamma' \not\in \Gamma'$, then we must use the contrapositive of Lemma \ref{cond2}.
nodes.statement_short: Check condition (2.4) via Lemma 3 plus the contrapositive of Lemma 1, then split condition (2.5) on whether $\gamma^*\in\Gamma'$.

nodes.name: Verify the vanishing-relation condition
nodes.statement: We have two conditions to check. The first, (\ref{ind1}), is taken as a direct consequence of Lemma \ref{gram} and the contrapositive of Lemma \ref{cond1}.
nodes.statement_short: Get the first condition from the Gram–Schmidt lemma and the contrapositive of Lemma 1.

nodes.name: Case $\gamma^* \in \Gamma'$
nodes.statement: (\ref{ind2}) must be broken up into two separate parts. If $\gamma^* \in \Gamma'$, then we may apply the contrapositive of Lemma \ref{cond1} again.
nodes.statement_short: For a target zero inside $\Gamma'$, reapply the contrapositive of Lemma 1.

nodes.name: Case $\gamma' \not\in \Gamma'$
nodes.statement: However, if $\gamma' \not\in \Gamma'$, then we must use the contrapositive of Lemma \ref{cond2}.
nodes.statement_short: For a target zero outside $\Gamma'$, use the contrapositive of Lemma 2 instead.

nodes.name: Why the natural basis fails and LLL-reduction is needed
nodes.statement: Therefore, given a basis for our lattice, we may determine a lower bound for $N_{\gamma}$. Note that we do not care which basis of the lattice we choose. At first glance, one may expect to take the basis given in Definition \ref{LKGamma}. However, if one attempts to perform the Gram--Schmidt on this basis, the vectors will be extremely {\it short}. It should only take a minute to convince the enthralled reader that even $|b_2^*|$ is relatively small. For this reason, we must find alternative bases for each lattice. Since there are many bases from which to choose we apply the LLL-reduction algorithm to find a {\it nearly orthogonal basis} for each lattice. By doing this, we will increase the length of the vectors obtained through the Gram--Schmidt orthogonalization process.
nodes.statement_short: The generating basis of $L(K;S)$ gives tiny Gram–Schmidt vectors, so an LLL-reduced nearly orthogonal basis is used instead.

nodes.name: LLL guarantee on successive Gram--Schmidt lengths
nodes.statement: By definition of LLL-reduction, once the basis is reduced via LLL-reduction, it is guaranteed that $$|b_p^*|^2 \geq |b_{p-1}^*|^2\left(\delta-\frac14\right)$$ for all permissible $p$.
assumptions: once the basis is reduced via LLL-reduction

nodes.name: Relative importance of the parameters $\delta$ and $k$
nodes.statement: These values are immensely important in our computation, since they give explicit information regarding the length of the shortest vector in the lattice. When computing the LLL-reduction, we tested several values of $\delta$ and $k$ to determine whether there was a significant difference in the choices. It turns out that the choice of $\delta$ is far less important than the choice of $k$. We refer the reader to \cite[Ch. 2]{computational-num-theory} for a closer look at LLL-reduction, including basically the same set up of vectors to determine the linear dependence of a set of numbers.

nodes.name: Computing and verifying the zeroes
nodes.statement: We chose $K = 10^k$ for some positive $k$: the $\gamma_i'$s are simply $\gamma_i$s accurate to $k$ decimal places (and then truncated). We used GP/Pari and Sage's functions that compute the zeroes. The programs were run independently, and we verified the zeroes using the intermediate value theorem on the Riemann $\xi$-function.

nodes.name: F\'{e}jer kernel
nodes.statement: In Theorem \ref{AndThm}, Anderson and Stark follow Ingham and use the F\'{e}jer kernel \begin{equation*} f(t) = \begin{cases} 1 - \frac{|t|}{T}, &\quad |t|\leq T, \\ 0, &\quad |t| >T \end{cases} \end{equation*} to truncate the relevant sums.

nodes.name: Requirements on a permissible truncating function
nodes.statement: A permissible function for such an endeavour is one which has a non-negative Fourier transform and is supported on $[-T, T]$, and which is `close' to unity in a neighbourhood about $t=0$. The last condition ensures that the contributions of the lower-lying zeroes are maximised.

nodes.name: Improved kernel $f_0$
nodes.statement: We use the function \begin{equation*} f_0(t) = \begin{cases} (1- \frac{|t|}{T})\cos \frac{\pi t}{T} + \pi^{-1}\sin\frac{\pi |t|}{T}, &\quad |t| \leq T, \\ 0, &\quad |t|>T \end{cases} \end{equation*} which is used by Odlyzko and te Riele in \cite{MertDis}
nodes.statement_short: The Odlyzko–te Riele kernel $(1-|t|/T)\cos(\pi t/T)+\pi^{-1}\sin(\pi|t|/T)$ supported on $[-T,T]$.

nodes.name: The heaviness ordering $\prec$ on the zeroes
nodes.statement: Since we want to maximize equation (\ref{AndS3}), we shall sort the zeroes based on the ordering $\prec$ defined as follows \begin{equation}\gamma_i \prec \gamma_j \iff \frac{1}{|\rho_{i} \zeta'(\rho_{i})|} f_0\left(\gamma_{i}\right) > \frac{1}{|\rho_{j} \zeta'(\rho_{j})|} f_0\left(\gamma_{j}\right).\end{equation} We shall say that $\gamma_i$ is {\it heavier} than $\gamma_j$ if $\gamma_i \prec \gamma_j$.
nodes.statement_short: $\gamma_i\prec\gamma_j$ when $\gamma_i$ contributes more weight $f_0(\gamma)/|\rho\zeta'(\rho)|$ to the bound.

nodes.name: Effect of the heaviness sort on the order of the zeroes
nodes.statement: For small values of $i$, sorting via $\prec$ does not seem to affect the order very much. However, as $T$ increases, the zeroes become scrambled.

nodes.name: Parameters and outcome of the main computation
nodes.statement: For our computation, we applied the main algorithm with $k = 9000$, $n = 500$ and $T \approx \gamma_{2001}-\epsilon$, where $\gamma_{2001}$ is the 2001st smallest zero. For the steps of the algorithm which required LLL-reduction, we used the standard $\delta = \frac34$ when performing LLL-reduction on $L_0$ and a weaker $\delta=\frac{3}{10}$ when reducing each $L_t$. Step 6 of the algorithm gave a candidate value for $N_\gamma$ of $794948$. When running the remaining 1500 zeroes through step 8, we find that the minimum candidate for $N_\gamma$ is $4976$.
nodes.statement_short: With $k=9000$, $n=500$ and $T\approx\gamma_{2001}-\epsilon$, step 6 gives $794948$ and step 8 lowers the minimum candidate to $4976$.

nodes.name: $\{N_\gamma\}$-independence of the heaviest 500 zeroes
nodes.statement: Let $\Gamma'$ be the heaviest 500 zeroes with $T=\gamma_{2001}-\epsilon$. Then the elements of $\Gamma'$ are $\{N_\gamma\}$-independent, where all $N_\gamma$s are $4976$.
conclusions: the elements of $\Gamma'$ are $\{N_\gamma\}$-independent, where all $N_\gamma$s are $4976$

nodes.name: Trade-off between the size of $\Gamma'$, of $K$, and running time
nodes.statement: Naturally, one should like to choose $\Gamma'$ to have as many entries as possible and $K$ to be as large as possible to improve on the bounds in Theorem \ref{Ours}. Unfortunately, the time taken to run each LLL-reduction is $O(n^{6}\log^3K) = O(n^6k^3)$, so either one of these choices may result in a quick computational explosion.

nodes.name: Running time of a single LLL-reduction
nodes.statement: the time taken to run each LLL-reduction is $O(n^{6}\log^3K) = O(n^6k^3)$
conclusions: the time taken to run each LLL-reduction is $O(n^{6}\log^3K) = O(n^6k^3)$

nodes.name: Effect of enlarging $n$ or $K$ on $N_\gamma$
nodes.statement: If we enlarge $n$ without changing $K$, the value of $N_\gamma$ is likely to decrease dramatically. Our experiments have shown that the value of $N_\gamma$ tends to drop to zero eventually as $n$ increases. On the flip-side, increasing the value of $K$ when the value of $N_\gamma$ is already large is relatively fruitless, as an increase of $K$ can only increase $N_\gamma$ and the $\frac{2N_\gamma}{N_\gamma+1}$ term is already close to $2$.

nodes.name: Taking a larger $T$ with re-sorting of the zeroes
nodes.statement: One might also suggest taking a larger value of $T$, re-sorting the zeroes and computing the corresponding $N_\gamma$. This seems to be the best possibility. By re-sorting the zeroes for each pair of $n$ and $T$, one has the {\it optimal} solution (provided the values of $N_\gamma$ remains large). However, if one wishes to roll the dice with different values of $n$ and $T$, one must do most of each computation from scratch. The first part of this recalculation can be cut down dramatically by storing specific intermediate results of the LLL-reduction and starting the reduction part way through. The second part of the recalculation, however, must be completely redone each time a new set of zeroes is selected.
nodes.statement_short: Re-sorting for each $(n,T)$ is optimal but forces most of the computation to be redone.

nodes.name: Height at which small values of $|\zeta'(\frac12+i\gamma)|$ appear
nodes.statement: in \cite{numeric-deriv}, it is stated that {\it small} values of $|\zeta'(\frac12+i\gamma)|$, about 0.002, do not appear until $|\gamma| \approx 10^{22}$

nodes.name: Stability of the sorted zeroes as $T \rightarrow \infty$
nodes.statement: Say we fix $n$ and we wish to send $T \rightarrow \infty$, sorting the zeroes once again for each selection of $T$. In order for a high zero to have a large contribution, its derivative must be small. However, in \cite{numeric-deriv}, it is stated that {\it small} values of $|\zeta'(\frac12+i\gamma)|$, about 0.002, do not appear until $|\gamma| \approx 10^{22}$, meaning that their contribution to the sum will be minuscule. Thus, once $T$ is raised past a {\it reasonable} height it is unlikely that the first $n$ sorted zeroes will change.

nodes.name: Figure 1: relationship between $n$ and $T$ with re-sorting
nodes.statement: Figure 1 shows the relationship between $n$ and $T$ with resorting of the zeroes. The chart assumes that $\frac{2N_\gamma}{N_\gamma+1} \approx 2$, which is a fair assumption if one believes that the zeroes are indeed linearly independent. Of special note, sorting the initial 9000 zeroes and taking the {\it best} 1000 in sorted order gives the first glimpse at improving Theorem \ref{Ours} by replacing 1.6383 with 2.
nodes.statement_short: Sorting the first 9000 zeroes and keeping the best 1000 would raise the constant $1.6383$ to $2$.

nodes.name: Figure 2: raising $T$ without re-sorting the zeroes
nodes.statement: To avoid the recomputation stated above, one may wish simply to increase the value of $T$ without resorting the zeroes. Unfortunately all this will accomplish is making the kernel closer to 1, meaning we will eventually hit a ceiling. For illustrative purposes, Figure 2 shows the value Theorem \ref{Ours} could obtain if one were to raise the value of $T$ (assuming that the value of $N_\gamma$ stays large). It uses the first 300 zeroes in sorted order (sorted using $T = \gamma_{2001}-\epsilon$), but $T$ varies. We also include the values that the F\'{e}jer kernel would produce.

nodes.name: The improved kernel needs far fewer zeroes than the F\'{e}jer kernel
nodes.statement: It is clear that the improved kernel approaches the maximal value quicker than the F\'{e}jer kernel. To obtain values within $0.01$ of the optimal value, the F\'{e}jer kernel needs to check a total of 30398 zeroes, while the improved kernel only needs to check 6224 zeroes. When a higher precision is needed, the gap widens immensely: to obtain values within $0.001$ of the optimal value, the F\'{e}jer kernel and the improved kernel need to check 399444 and 24043 zeroes, respectively.
nodes.statement_short: To reach $0.001$ of the optimum the Fejér kernel needs 399444 zeroes against 24043 for the improved kernel.
conclusions: the F\'{e}jer kernel and the improved kernel need to check 399444 and 24043 zeroes, respectively

nodes.name: Trade-off in the choice of $\delta$ for LLL-reduction
nodes.statement: There is also a trade-off when determining which value to take for $\delta$ in the LLL-reduction. As we took more zeroes, the differences really started to shine through. Taking larger values of $\delta$ yielded a slower program, but one that gave a much better value for $N_{\gamma}$. On the other hand, taking a smaller value of $\delta$ sped up the program, but gave much smaller values for $N_{\gamma}$.

nodes.name: Dropping the assumption that all $N_\gamma$ are equal
nodes.statement: Finally, we have assumed that each of the $N_\gamma$s be the same. This is not necessary for our method to work. The bound in Lemma \ref{cond1} may be rewritten as $$|v|^2 < 2\max(N_\gamma) + 1 + \left(1+\sum N_{\gamma}\right)^2 + \sum N_{\gamma}^2.$$ A similar bound may be drawn up for Lemma \ref{cond2}. These bounds, however, are only useful when the resulting value of $N_{\gamma}$ from Theorem \ref{cond3} is relatively small.
nodes.statement_short: The Lemma 1 bound generalises to unequal $N_\gamma$, but is only useful when the resulting $N_\gamma$ is small.

nodes.name: Grosswald's Theorem 1 on sign changes of $\pi(x)-\mathrm{li}(x)$
nodes.statement: in \cite{Grosswald}, Theorem 1 gives us that $\pi(x) - \textrm{li}(x)$ changes sign infinitely often provided that the first 30 zeroes are $5$-independent

nodes.name: Grosswald's Theorem 2 on the P\'{o}lya and Tur\'{a}n functions
nodes.statement: Theorem 2 shows that the functions associated with conjectures of P\'{o}lya and Tur\'{a}n, respectively \begin{equation*} L(x) = \sum_{1\leq n \leq x} \lambda(n), \quad T(x) = \sum_{1\leq n \leq x} \frac{\lambda(n)}{n}, \end{equation*} where $\lambda(n)$ is the Liouville function, change sign infinitely often provided that the first 13 zeroes are $16$-independent.
nodes.statement_short: $L(x)=\sum\lambda(n)$ and $T(x)=\sum\lambda(n)/n$ change sign infinitely often if the first 13 zeroes are $16$-independent.

nodes.name: New proofs of the Grosswald results from Table 2
nodes.statement: The data provided in Table \ref{n-indep} are more than enough to provide new proofs of these results.

nodes.name: Table 1: smallest sums with coefficients $-1,0,1$
nodes.statement: Table \ref{one-indep} gives the smallest sum (in absolute value) of the first $N$ zeroes of the zeta-function using coefficients $|c_n| \leq 1$. We have checked all permissible sums up to $N=41$. The first $20$ zeroes were checked in \cite[Table I]{Bateman}, labelled as {\it Type (A)}. They also provide a probabilistic value for the minimum value of such a sum, which we also include below.

nodes.name: Encoding of a linear combination as an ordered pair of integers
nodes.statement: To avoid a lengthy column of $\gamma$s to show the smallest linear combination, we encode the sums by an ordered pair of integers. If you write each integer in terms of its binary representation, a $1$ in the $i$th least significant bit implies that $\gamma_i$ is in the sum. The $i$th least significant bit being a $1$ in the first (resp. second) coordinate gives us a positive (resp. negative) coefficient.
nodes.statement_short: Two integers encode a $\pm1/0$ combination: bit $i$ of the first (second) integer marks $\gamma_i$ with coefficient $+1$ ($-1$).

nodes.name: The encoded pair $(5,24)$
nodes.statement: For example, $(5,24)$ represents the sum $\gamma_1+\gamma_3-\gamma_4-\gamma_5$.

nodes.name: $m$-independence
nodes.statement: By $m$-independence here, we mean that all non-trivial linear combinations of the first $n$ zeroes are nonzero assuming the coefficients are no more than $m$ in absolute value.
nodes.statement_short: The first $n$ zeroes are $m$-independent if no nontrivial integer combination with coefficients at most $m$ vanishes.

nodes.name: Table 2: new lower bounds on $m$-independence
nodes.statement: Table \ref{n-indep} gives us new lower bounds on the $m$-independence of the first $n$ zeroes of the zeta-function.

nodes.name: Method and coverage of the $m$-independence table
nodes.statement: This was computed using the same method as above, but keeping the zeroes in cardinal order. We include full results for the first 20 zeroes, and then only specific entries past there. Note that if $k$ is not included in the table, any bound for the first $n > k$ zeroes also gives a lower bound for the first $k$ zeroes.
